summary: This informational document defines four extendable-output functions (hash functions with output of any length): TurboSHAKE128, TurboSHAKE256, KT128 and KT256. All are efficient, and the KT functions can take advantage of parallel hardware.

eli5.summary: A hash function squeezes any amount of data into a short fingerprint. These four make fingerprints of whatever length you want and are built to be fast.

subtitle: Fast, parallelizable hash functions with variable-length output.

tldr.problem: SHA-3 and SHAKE hash functions process data serially and cannot take advantage of modern CPUs with parallel execution. For large messages, serial processing leaves significant computing power unused.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines four new extendable-output functions (XOFs): TurboSHAKE128, TurboSHAKE256 (which are faster SHAKE variants using 12 rounds instead of 24), and KT128, KT256 (which add tree hashing on top of TurboSHAKE to exploit parallelism). KangarooTwelve (KT128/KT256) splits large messages into 8192-byte chunks, hashes them in parallel, and combines the results.
tldr.outcome: These functions are roughly twice as fast as SHAKE for the same security level. KT128 and KT256 can process large messages much faster on parallel hardware while incurring no overhead for short messages. The RFC is an informational IRTF research result.

today: RFC 9861 is an Informational document from the IRTF Crypto Forum Research Group. It is not an Internet Standard but provides a stable reference and implementation guide for TurboSHAKE and KangarooTwelve. These functions have been registered in IANA's COSE algorithm registry for use in cryptographic applications, and implementations are available in several libraries.

sections.title: The Challenge of Efficient Hashing
sections.content:
Modern cryptography relies on hash functions to compress data of any size into a short fingerprint (digest). These fingerprints uniquely identify data: change even one bit and the hash changes completely. Hash functions are used for digital signatures, message authentication, key derivation, and many other applications.

The SHA-3 standard defines SHAKE functions (SHAKE128 and SHAKE256), which are extendable-output functions (XOFs) that can produce output of any length. However, SHAKE processes data in a single stream, unable to take advantage of modern CPUs that can perform multiple operations in parallel.

This RFC defines faster alternatives: TurboSHAKE (faster versions of SHAKE with fewer rounds) and KangarooTwelve (tree hashing on top of TurboSHAKE). KangarooTwelve can parallelize the hashing of large messages, making it up to several times faster than SHAKE on modern multi-core systems.
sections.eli5: Hashing is like making a fingerprint of data. These functions make fingerprints fast, and some can use multiple processors at once to go even faster.

sections.title: TurboSHAKE: Faster Keccak Hashing
sections.content:
TurboSHAKE is a family of XOFs based on a round-reduced version of the Keccak permutation used in SHA-3. Instead of the standard 24 rounds, TurboSHAKE uses only 12 rounds, making it roughly twice as fast while maintaining the same security strength.

The RFC defines two instances: TurboSHAKE128 (aiming for 128-bit security) and TurboSHAKE256 (aiming for 256-bit security). Both use the sponge construction: a message is absorbed (XORed into a state), the permutation is applied, and then output is squeezed out. The number of output bytes can be arbitrary, making them true extendable-output functions.

TurboSHAKE128 uses a rate of 168 bytes (1344 bits) and capacity of 32 bytes (256 bits). TurboSHAKE256 uses a rate of 136 bytes (1088 bits) and capacity of 64 bytes (512 bits). A domain separation byte in the input allows protocols to create independent instances of the function for different purposes without calling it multiple times.

Because TurboSHAKE uses fewer rounds, its security relies on cryptanalysis of 12-round Keccak. Extensive cryptanalysis of Keccak provides confidence that the reduced-round version is also secure.
sections.eli5: TurboSHAKE is like a faster version of a standard hash function. By skipping some steps, it makes fingerprints twice as fast without getting less secure.

sections.title: KangarooTwelve: Parallel Tree Hashing
sections.content:
KangarooTwelve (KT128 and KT256) applies tree hashing on top of TurboSHAKE. The key innovation is parallelization: large messages are split into chunks, each chunk is hashed independently in parallel, and the digests are combined.

For messages larger than 8192 bytes, KangarooTwelve splits the message into 8192-byte chunks. Each chunk (except the first) is hashed separately with TurboSHAKE, producing a 32-byte (for KT128) or 64-byte (for KT256) digest. These digests, along with the first chunk, are combined into a final node, which is then hashed with TurboSHAKE to produce the output.

For messages of 8192 bytes or less, KangarooTwelve simply hashes the message directly with TurboSHAKE, incurring no parallelization overhead.

The tree hashing mode uses Sakura coding, a scheme that ensures soundness of tree hashing: the hash of a tree structure is different from the hash of a flat message that happens to have the same bytes. This prevents ambiguity and collisions from different tree structures producing the same output.

Both KT128 and KT256 accept an optional customization string that allows different versions of the function for different applications (similar to TurboSHAKE's domain separation byte but with more flexibility).
sections.eli5: For a big message, split it into pieces, hash each piece on separate processors, then hash all the fingerprints together. This makes hashing large files very fast on modern computers.

sections.title: Security Properties and Advantages
sections.content:
TurboSHAKE128 and KT128 provide 128-bit security, equivalent to SHAKE128. TurboSHAKE256 and KT256 provide 256-bit security, equivalent to SHAKE256. When output length is long enough (256 bits for 128-bit security, 512 bits for 256-bit security), these functions meet NIST's requirements for post-quantum security levels 2 and 5 respectively.

Unlike SHA-256 and SHA-512, these functions do not suffer from length extension attacks, where an attacker who knows the hash of a message can compute the hash of the message appended with additional data. This makes them suitable for direct use in message authentication without the HMAC construction.

The RFC also defines a HopMAC construction for message authentication: hash the key and message together using a two-layer approach. Because the inner hash is keyless, only the outer hash layer needs protection against side-channel attacks, simplifying implementation.

On modern hardware with SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) support, KT128 and KT256 can process messages significantly faster than ParallelHash (the only other parallel hash function in NIST standards), while having no overhead for short messages.
sections.eli5: These functions are safe against tricks that some hash functions fall for. They're easy to use for protecting messages, and computers can run them super fast.

viz.caption: Advantages of KangarooTwelve vs standard hash functions

items.title: Parallelizable
items.text: Large messages are split into chunks hashed independently, exploiting multi-core CPUs.

items.title: No short-message overhead
items.text: Messages under 8192 bytes are hashed directly without parallel tree construction.

items.title: Fast XOF
items.text: Produces output of any length as fast as input is processed, unlike SHA-256-based MGF.

items.title: No length extension attacks
items.text: Safe for direct MAC use without requiring the HMAC construction.
